title: Fordlandia: Brazil Isn't Michigan
summary: Hosts Josh and Chuck (iHeart Intro voice) cover Fordlandia, Henry Ford's failed rubber plantation and planned utopian company town in the Brazilian Amazon along the Tapajos River. They trace Ford's vertical integration ideas, his earlier failed Muscle Shoals project in Alabama, the rubber market after the Stevenson Plan, the 1927 land grant, the chaotic early management, the cafeteria riot and occupation, the rigid imposition of Midwestern culture, the later manager Archibald Johnston, the move to Belterra, and the sale back to Brazil. The episode ends with a plug for their kids book and a brief tangent about movies.
topics: South American leaf blight and rubber pests

segments.title: Opening and sources
segments.summary: The hosts introduce the episode, a listener suggestion from Brennan Wilson, and credit the book by Greg Grandin and a 1970s paper by John Gallagher on Fordlandia.

segments.title: Henry Ford's character and industrial ideas
segments.summary: Overview of Henry Ford's oddities, including his paternalistic employee oversight through the Sociology Department, anti-Semitic writings, square dancing, soy enthusiasm, and his embrace of vertical integration and the assembly line.

segments.title: Muscle Shoals attempt
segments.summary: In 1921 Ford tried to lease the Wilson Dam area near Muscle Shoals, Alabama, with its World War One nitrate facilities, for five million dollars. An Alabama senator opposed it, and the deal collapsed; Ford was threatened and had armed bodyguards.

segments.title: Rubber history and the Asian rubber plantations
segments.summary: Brazil dominated the rubber trade from the Amazon until rubber trees were transplanted to Sri Lanka and Southeast Asia, where pests were absent, and Brazil's rubber economy collapsed.

segments.title: Stevenson Plan and the 1927 land grant
segments.summary: The British Stevenson Plan restricted rubber supply, prompting Herbert Hoover to push for American rubber. Ford received a gift of about two and a half million acres on the Tapajos River in 1927, with a negotiated royalty arrangement and reported kickbacks.

segments.title: Ford's motives and the Dutch rubber market
segments.summary: Ford's stated rubber motive was tire supply, but he was driven more by a utopian vision. The Dutch undercut the British, making a Ford plantation seem unnecessary to rubber experts.

segments.title: Founding of Fordlandia and early problems
segments.summary: Shipping supplies upriver took about nine to ten months. Einar Oxholm, a Danish steamship captain with no experience, became manager. The town began as Boa Vista and was renamed Fordlandia. Ford's team lacked plant expertise, and attempts to control leaf blight with imported leaf-cutter ants failed.

segments.title: Early failure report
segments.summary: A September 1929 troubleshooter reported a complete lack of organization, and the Brazilian agriculture minister reportedly considered the project a waste of money.

segments.title: Town amenities and segregation
segments.summary: Ford built hospitals, a water tower, pools, golf courses, generators, and sawmills, but the American staff's area was separated from Brazilian workers, who had poorer housing and well water and were paid about 35 cents a day.

segments.title: Cultural imposition and medical practices
segments.summary: Ford imposed American diet, housing, an eight-hour day, and bans on drinking, clashing with local work rhythms, hammock sleeping, and midwifery. A doctor interviewed in 1994 described withholding food from pregnant women to push hospital births. The hosts reflect on rigid projects failing to adapt to local conditions.

segments.title: The cafeteria riot and occupation
segments.summary: Workers protested a switch from table service to a cafeteria line after a supervisor laughed at Manuel Costa de Jesus. Workers rioted, wrecked buildings and equipment, and occupied the town for three days until Brazilian military, arranged through Pan American, suppressed the uprising. Workers were then fired.

segments.title: Archibald Johnston and Belterra
segments.summary: Manager Archibald Johnston, nicknamed the white tiger, adapted to local conditions and improved roads, houses, schools, and a theater. Plant pathologist James Weir then moved operations to the new Belterra plantation in 1934, which produced some rubber but far short of Ford's needs.

segments.title: Sale of Fordlandia and Ford family history
segments.summary: Ford gave up making its own tires in 1942. Edsel Ford became a figurehead and tried to sell the project as early as 1935. Edsel died in 1943 after drinking unpasteurized milk from a Ford farm. Henry Ford II cleaned house and sold Fordlandia back to Brazil. Henry Ford's cow hatred is mentioned.

segments.title: Aftermath and modern Fordlandia
segments.summary: Synthetic rubber ended the rubber tree's usefulness. Fordlandia remains partly standing, and thousands of people now live there and in Belterra, working with gypsum deposits discovered after Ford left. Brazilians consider these inhabited cities, not abandoned ones.

segments.title: Movie tangent
segments.summary: The hosts briefly joke about casting a movie about Fordlandia, with Sam Rockwell and Margot Robbie mentioned, and discuss other films.

segments.title: Kids book plug
segments.summary: The hosts promote their children's book Stuff Kids Should Know, published with Macmillan and co-written with Nils Parker.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: The hosts invite listener email and sign off with the show's production credit.
